abstract: {middle dot} In evergreen conifers, late-season photosynthetic downregulation is typically coordinated with growth cessation and the induction of cold acclimation, a key component of winter adaptation. However, the transcriptional basis of this coordination and its sensitivity to warming and drought remain poorly understood. {middle dot} To investigate the molecular basis of these responses, we examined how summer drought, autumn warming and their combination affect the expression of photosynthetic and cold-acclimation genes in white spruce, and whether responses differ among families from different latitudes. {middle dot} Autumn warming sustained photosynthetic gene expression into early winter while suppressing cold-acclimation genes, demonstrating that photosynthetic and cold-acclimation networks become decoupled from growth cessation, which remained largely unchanged. Although cold acclimation models derived from herbaceous species predict regulation through CBF pathways, canonical CBF/DREB regulators showed little transcriptional response. Instead, warming-induced suppression of cold acclimation was mediated by MYB- and AP2/ERF-centered regulatory networks, indicating a distinct conifer mechanism. Northern and southern families also differed in their transcriptional responses to warming despite exhibiting similar growth-cessation phenology. {middle dot} Together, these findings identify regulatory networks through which warmer autumns disrupt seasonal coordination in boreal conifers, potentially increasing susceptibility to freezing injury, limiting spring recovery, and ultimately affecting forest carbon sequestration.
